title: High Tibial Osteotomy Versus Total Knee Arthroplasty for Knee Osteoarthritis in Patients Aged 65 Years or Younger: A Propensity Score–Matched Cohort Study at a Regional Non-Teaching Hospital
content: Background/Objectives: High tibial osteotomy (HTO) preserves the native knee, but its outcomes relative to total knee arthroplasty (TKA) in younger patients remain uncertain. We compared clinical outcomes at a regional non-teaching hospital in Thailand. Methods: This observational cohort combined retrospective record review with prospective in-person assessment of patients aged ≤65 years who underwent TKA or HTO for knee osteoarthritis between 2013 and 2025. Knees were propensity score–matched 1:1. Outcome models adjusted for Kellgren–Lawrence grade and follow-up duration. Equivalence margins were based on published minimal clinically important differences. Results: Of 291 knees (204 TKA and 87 HTO), 98 were matched in 49 pairs. Compared with TKA, HTO was associated with higher visual analogue scale pain scores (adjusted mean difference, 0.7 points; 95% confidence interval (CI), 0.1–1.3), greater maximum flexion (11.3°; 95% CI, 6.4–16.2), and higher Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) Sport/Recreation scores (19.8 points; 95% CI, 7.8–31.9). Timed Up and Go and 20-m walk completion times were longer after HTO by 2.4 and 4.1 seconds, respectively. The Hospital for Special Surgery knee score and KOOS Pain, Symptoms, Activities of Daily Living, and Quality of Life subscales met the equivalence criteria. Conclusions: HTO was associated with greater knee motion and better self-reported sports function, whereas TKA was associated with less pain and faster timed mobility. These trade-offs support individualized treatment selection, including HTO for joint preservation.
